video.title: AI researchers debate how close we are to recursive self-improvement

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Whisper small transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: The hype cycle: a new model comes out, people say 'this is AGI', and a month later it feels dumb, because you stay bottlenecked where it is weak. Opens on 'there's this cycle that keeps repeating' (skipping 'Yeah, so'); lands on 'maybe there are just more of these cycles than we'd expect'. Opening at 109.7 on 'Humans have a lot of advantages over models' also works but is longer.

Host's intuition pump: chess engine Elo rose in a straight line since the 80s, yet looked like a sudden jump once it crossed the human range. Opens on 'if you look at the Elo score of chess bots' (after 'Or another intuition pump is'); lands on 'that's just because they're slowly rising in Elo relative to humans'.

John Schulman (says 'early OpenAI days') on his old belief that minimizing next-token log loss could never produce intelligence, because the important bits are too small a part of the loss. Payoff: 'but then it turned out that it just worked anyway.'

Likely John: humans' last job is defining the objective and deciding what we want: RLHF objectives, constitutions, model specs. Opens on the claim itself; lands on 'decide what we actually want'. Dwarkesh's one-line 'Alignment is the final job' (to 992.8) is an acceptable button.

Q: why is there no huge consolidation among model providers? Answer: distillation. Anything learned through RL is a few bits and easy to distill from trajectories. Opens on the question just after the Antithesis ad; lands on 'you can easily distill it'. The line after it only restates the point.

Hot take: 'isn't it weird how Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 are almost objectively worse than GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3', despite having logit distillation from Mythos, which suggests frontier labs have little edge in RL environments. Lands when another voice finishes it with 'real-world deployment matters more than the environment' (misheard as 'the real world of playing').

How Cursor's Composer does online RL: tab accepted or not, one rollout per user so variance has to be estimated by heuristics, and a new model ships every five hours if it beats Cursor Bench. Lands on 'if it didn't, they would throw that version out.'

Surprising fact: a model trained only on pre-1930 text, fine-tuned on coding-agent data, beat Claude 3 Opus on SWE-bench. So once you have examples of expert behavior they copy easily into a weak model. Lands on 'surprisingly easy to copy that into a relatively weak model'. The counterexample that follows opens 'But a counter example to that' and is a separate beat.

Where training signal comes from. In pretraining it is already in Common Crawl and the job is filtering, but later 'there's no hidden proof of the Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl we can just filter until we see it.' Both ends work: 3955.5 lands the punchline; 3973.1 adds the conclusion 'you have to get the bits from somewhere' (humans, environments, deployment).

Host's own study: every training recipe from 2019 to now crossed with every dataset from 2019 to now. At small scale, data explains about 9x of compute-efficiency gains and architecture about 3x. Opens on the question 'how much of pretraining progress is driven by data'; lands on the numbers.

Likely John: models seem good at writing, but a distributional analysis shows reused themes and the same character names, one good style. And since everyone distills from Claude, all open-weight models write like Claude, 'this monoculture'. Opening at 5206.1 adds 'diversity is lower after RL' but begins 'Then there's another way'. Opening at 5209 would start on 'their', so avoid it.

Rapid-fire question: when do we get an AI that beats top human experts at all computer work, even three-year projects, 'basically ASI'. A guest says 'three or four years', the host says 'The fuck?', and a second guest says 'that doesn't seem wrong'. Ending on 'The fuck?' (5686.3) also works; 5690.5 includes the second beat after the laugh.

also_ok.why: Moore's law looked like a straight line, but it needed many discrete innovations. LLMs are the same (pretraining, then RL), and today's RL recipe may not find the next discontinuity. Clear, but abstract.

Host: before each seven-figure experiment, spend as much compute on AI labor, a 'century' of thinking. Guest answers 'we're nowhere near the ceiling of how well you can do research'. Works, but long and wordy.

Thinking can't create new bits, but with a well-specified objective an AI would have caught the Kaplan scaling-law annealing mistake and saved a year or two. It could give a 10x speedup, but it doesn't help find the right objective. Close to the top of the band.

Distilling is hard even with full model access, because you need a realistic prompt distribution. Router or proxy services that let people in China use US frontier models collect and sell that data, the perfect prompt distribution.

Host retells asking Dario: if models will learn on the job, why bake in PowerPoint skills? Two readings: models aren't there yet, or it is revenue to fund RSI and the post-singularity model will be good at everything. ('We've been ahead of Dario' is misheard 'We had Dario'.)
John: much of what people call taste is knowing which behavior works in the long run, e.g. which software systems stay maintainable. Short and crisp, near the bottom of the band.

RL didn't give horizontal generalization (math doesn't make you a coder), but it did give horizon generalization: models keep making progress over more tokens, and time horizons double every three months. The speaker's 'first thing' framing leaves a second point after the cut.

negatives.why: Intro of guests and their labs: housekeeping, not a point.
Antithesis sponsor read. It sounds on-topic (agents, the verification bottleneck) but it is an ad.
Minecraft banter ('isn't it crazy we call that too easy', 'I did that five years ago'). A room moment that riffs on the previous line.
GrokBot sponsor read, about finding clips in transcripts. Tempting and on-theme, but an ad.
'27x vs 2000x, where's the missing 100x.' Numbers that only mean something after the data-vs-architecture study a minute earlier.
Rapid fire: 'somewhere between five and 10 years', 'Oh really?', a mix-up over definitions. The answers are cut off from the question and depend on the earlier framing.
